transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-29 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Morales (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Omar Chen (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Cenova VP Eng), Samir Khan (Cenova Platform), Diane Ho (Cenova Security), Eliot Park (Cenova SRE)

Summary (auto): Initial discovery on availability architecture and incident tolerance. Customer wants concrete pilots to validate failover and latency.

00:00:05 - Lena Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, I'll kick us off. We wanted to understand your availability targets and what tradeoffs you're willing to accept between latency and cost.
00:00:18 - Marta Ruiz: Thanks Lena. Uh hi team. High level, we have two product flows; user-facing chat (latency sensitive) and nightly batch inference (throughput). Primary ask is the chat path - 99.9 p99 SLA ideally under 250 milliseconds, and we need geo failover inside EU/US only due to data residency.
00:00:40 - Ravi Patel: Okay that helps. Quick clarifying q — when you say p99 250 ms, is that client-perceived RTT or server-side token generation?
00:00:48 - Samir Khan: That's end-to-end, so user to model generation back to client. There's network overhead but we measure from edge.
00:00:55 - Ravi Patel: Got it. So Redwood offers multiple options — hosted API for fast onboarding, Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for air-gapped/regulatory. Each has different routing and SLA capabilities.
00:01:10 - Diane Ho: Security is a blocker for Hosted if we can't show tenant-level at-rest encryption and customer-managed keys. SOC2 is fine but we need KMS/HSM control and audit logs.
00:01:22 - Omar Chen: Understood. Hosted supports BYOK with our KMS integrations and we can provide per-tenant audit trails, but for certain customers we recommend Dedicated or Private when you need zero shared tenancy risk.
00:01:36 - Eliot Park: From an ops perspective we want graceful degradation not hard failure. E.g., if model latency spikes we want automatic fallback to a smaller distilled model with degraded quality but preserved responsiveness, and also a cached response for repeated prompts.
00:01:51 - Ravi Patel: Yes, we have a multi-tier fallback policy pattern — primary high-quality model, a mid-tier quantized variant, and a micro distilled model. On route saturation we can roll traffic to the next tier and optionally serve cached prefixes. We also offer prefix/KV cache priming so you don't pay cold-start token costs.
00:02:10 - Marta Ruiz: How does multi-region steering work? We need EU-region first, but if EU capacity is exhausted or there's an AZ outage, traffic should failover to another EU region only — not to US. Can you pin residency and restrict cross-region failover?
00:02:26 - Omar Chen: You can pin region and we support region-level policies. You can configure allowed failover regions, plus a policy engine to block non-compliant cross-region fallback. On Hosted we handle routing but you'll be able to specify geo policies; Dedicated gives you more control on placement.
00:02:44 - Marta Ruiz: Is there a mechanism to route by latency versus cost? Like prefer local region unless latency threshold exceeded then route to a colder region?
00:02:53 - Ravi Patel: Yes, smart routing policies can be latency-first, cost-first, or strict-residency. You can set SLO-based routing: e.g., if P95 > 200ms for 30s, divert new sessions to alternate region. That's how we implement graceful degradation at routing layer.
00:03:08 - Samir Khan: On Dedicated, what's the guarantee for throughput and preemption? We need reserved throughput for peak windows.
00:03:15 - Omar Chen: Dedicated is committed capacity — you get reserved GPUs and predictable throughput. We allow burst capacity, but that’s subject to pool availability. For true isolation and predictable tail latency, Dedicated or Private is recommended.
00:03:28 - Diane Ho: For pilot can Hosted be used and then migrate to Dedicated? We're trying to avoid big upfront commit without validation.
00:03:35 - Lena Morales: Absolutely. A common pattern is to start hosted for speed of validation, instrument the workloads then design reserved capacity for production. We typically run a short pilot to validate latency/failover and then propose a Dedicated sizing and pricing.
00:03:47 - 00:04:10 - Speaker 1 (transcription glitch): Yeah, so the the part where um when the the, sorry.
00:04:12 - Ravi Patel: No worries. On the topic of failure modes, we run chaos scenarios in our own infra tests, but for customers we recommend simple runbooks: circuit breakers at the routing layer (reject or queue), model fallbacks, cached responses, and an operator alerting cadence.
00:04:30 - Eliot Park: Do you support partial degradation? E.g., keep short responses fast and batch longer ones, or reduce sampling/top-p to speed tokens?
00:04:38 - Omar Chen: Yes you can configure degraded profiles: lower max_tokens, lower temperature, or switch to a faster quantized model. You can also implement token-level throttling: cap tokens per second to preserve headroom.
00:04:50 - Marta Ruiz: Auditability — how do we prove which model generated a response and who accessed keys? We need immutable logs for later forensics.
00:04:58 - Ravi Patel: We emit audit logs for every inference call: model version, config, caller token, and request metadata. Those are exportable to your SIEM and we support long-term retention (add-on). For critical regulatory customers we integrate with customer KMS and HSM for key operations.
00:05:18 - Samir Khan: Any recommendations to reduce cold-starts for rare queries? We have a non-uniform traffic distribution.
00:05:24 - Omar Chen: Cold-starts are reduced by KV/prefix caching and by keeping warmed worker pools for hot routes. For rare routes you can pre-warm based on scheduled traffic or use small on-demand workers with quicker startup. We also support model snapshots with warmed KV cache for canary starts.
00:05:38 - 00:06:05 - [crosstalk] Speaker 2: yeah -- that, that makes sense.
00:06:07 - Lena Morales: Let's talk about SLO enforcement and penalties. What does Cenova expect versus what Redwood provides?
00:06:14 - Marta Ruiz: We're early but procurement will require an SLA table. For chat flows we want percentage uptime and a P99 latency SLO. If you could outline our failure modes that qualify for credits that will help.
00:06:27 - Ravi Patel: We have standard SLA templates: uptime SLAs for Dedicated and Private with credits for sustained downtime windows. Hosted has a best-effort SLA for latency, but Dedicated/Private can offer contractual P99 latency targets tied to reserved capacity. We'll share a sample SLA contract.
00:06:41 - Diane Ho: Is there an objective way to map incidents to root cause if there's a cross-stack issue— say network vs model vs infra?
00:06:49 - Omar Chen: Yes, our console provides per-route traces, model-level metrics (queue time, token gen time), and infra telemetry (GPU utilization, host-level). We also include request-level traces to correlate. For pilot we can enable detailed traces for a short retention window to help triage.
00:07:03 - Samir Khan: How would rollback or canary work during model upgrades? We don't want a model change to take down the chat path.
00:07:09 - Ravi Patel: We support staged rollouts: canary at 1-5%, monitoring evaluation metrics and automated rollback thresholds. You can pair that with traffic-splitting and automatic fallback to previous model if regressions detected.
00:07:21 - Marta Ruiz: If an AZ goes down, how fast is failover? We're targeting seamless recovery under 60s ideally for new sessions.
00:07:29 - Omar Chen: Varies with caching and session affinity. If you use stateless requests we can failover almost immediately, but sessions with KV cache might see initial slower responses as cache repopulates. With prefix caching and warmed pools, failover can be under 30-60s. We can model that in the pilot.
00:07:45 - 00:08:10 - Eliot Park: What about cost increases during failover? If we route to a more expensive region or spin extra capacity, how is that billed?
00:08:17 - Lena Morales: We track per-route cost in the console. For Hosted, costs are usage-based; for Dedicated you'd pay for reserved plus any burst at a premium. We can also include a failover policy that prefers cost-friendly options but will override for SLO breaches.
00:08:31 - Marta Ruiz: We need an estimate for pilot vs production — rough numbers are fine.
00:08:36 - Ravi Patel: We'll share a pilot pricing sheet. Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks with limited reserved capacity and a small usage bucket on Hosted to validate. Production Dedicated sizing depends on your p95/p99 targets and concurrency; we'll run a right-sizing exercise after we see your traffic CSV.
00:08:50 - Samir Khan: In terms of observability, can we push raw traces into our Datadog?
00:08:55 - Omar Chen: Yes, we support exports to Datadog/Prometheus/Splunk and structured logs to S3 or your SIEM. You can also set tracing hooks for end-to-end correlation.
00:09:05 - 00:09:30 - [short pause — team reviewing materials on screen]
00:09:33 - Diane Ho: A compliance question — for Private deployments, what parts of the control plane remain with Redwood? We want to know exactly what is customer-managed.
00:09:41 - Ravi Patel: For Private we ship a customer-managed control plane or a hybrid depending on the option. There's a fully on-prem package where you manage the runtime and keys; Redwood provides the orchestration tooling and optional support plane. We can run through the deployment matrix in the follow-up doc.
00:09:57 - Marta Ruiz: Are there any production incidents from other customers that are relevant? Like typical mitigations?
00:10:03 - Lena Morales: We anonymize postmortems but common patterns are: sudden traffic spikes causing queueing (mitigated by circuit breakers and token rate limits), model regressions after an untested rollout (mitigated by canary + evals), and AZ-level network flaps (mitigated by multi-AZ placement and prefix caching).
00:10:20 - Samir Khan: For pilot, can you run simulated AZ outage tests so we can see exactly how traffic reroutes?
00:10:26 - Omar Chen: Yes, we can run controlled failover tests in the pilot and produce a runbook. We'll simulate region and AZ-level outages and observe latency/availability metrics.
00:10:36 - 00:11:00 - Speaker 3 (auto-label): um hmm yeah thats good
00:11:02 - Lena Morales: Quick note on model variants: switching across quantized or distilled variants will change output fidelity. We recommend having an automatic fallthrough test set so you can measure quality delta on fallback. We can run regressions against your eval set during pilot.
00:11:18 - Marta Ruiz: That would be helpful. We have an in-house eval and we'll share a small subset for pilot.
00:11:23 - Ravi Patel: Great. About long tail cold starts: if you have rare intents we can pre-generate embeddings or cache canonical responses for those flows to avoid slow generation.
00:11:32 - Samir Khan: Any limits on number of routes for Dedicated? We have many micro-services calling model endpoints.
00:11:38 - Omar Chen: You can define multiple routes; Dedicated supports high cardinality but design matters — each route can have its own warmed pool and caching policy; that affects capacity planning.
00:11:50 - 00:12:20 - [typing audible, background noise]
00:12:22 - Diane Ho: If we go Dedicated and want on-prem later, is there a migration path?
00:12:27 - Ravi Patel: Yes, we support migration. We try to keep the API and config consistent so you can migrate from Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private with minimal app changes. Key migration points are KMS and network configuration.
00:12:36 - Eliot Park: For incident alerting thresholds, what do you recommend we monitor?
00:12:41 - Omar Chen: Monitor queue depth, worker utilization, p95/p99 latency, error rates, and token error codes. Also monitor model regression signals (n-gram overlap changes, embedding drift) if you have quality guardrails.
00:12:55 - Marta Ruiz: For the pilot scope, we need a clear success criteria doc — e.g., p99 < 250ms 99.9% of time during business hours, failover under 60s, no data exfiltration, KMS in place.
00:13:07 - Lena Morales: We'll draft a pilot success criteria with pass/fail thresholds and attach the benchmark harness.
00:13:12 - 00:13:35 - [brief side conversation about calendar scheduling — inaudible]
00:13:36 - Samir Khan: One more curious thing — does Redwood provide any tooling to auto-suggest quantization levels or batch sizes?
00:13:44 - Ravi Patel: Yes, Redwood Optimize recommends batching, quantization, and model variant suggestions based on workload traces. It can recommend a quantization profile that balances latency and output similarity.
00:13:55 - Marta Ruiz: Excellent. Ok last thing before wrap — what's a realistic timeline from pilot sign-off to Dedicated production?
00:14:02 - Omar Chen: Typically 6-8 weeks: pilot 2-4 weeks, sizing + procurement 1-2 weeks, Dedicated provisioning + validation 2-3 weeks. Private/on-prem can add more depending on your infra.
00:14:14 - Lena Morales: Perfect. We'll circle back with the pilot proposal and security packet.
00:14:19 - 00:14:40 - [wrap-up, attendees exchange thanks]

Recap / Next steps:
- Redwood to send SOC2, ISO, KMS integration docs and sample SLA (Lena)
- Redwood SE (Ravi/Omar) to draft pilot benchmark plan and runbook and schedule failover tests (Ravi)
- Cenova to share traffic profile and eval subset (Marta)
- Cenova security to list compliance artifacts and any required controls (Diane)

End of transcript.
